While shortening the adsorption time to one hour may reduce the total amount of CO₂ captured per cycle, it enables faster cycling and increases the number of DAC cycles per unit time. This reduction in capacity can be partially mitigated by increasing the adsorption airflow rate—provided the rate of CO₂ capture remains sufficiently high. As shown in Figure 34, breakthrough curves were compared across three airflow rates (up to 150% of the baseline). When limiting the adsorption time to one hour, increasing the airflow rate improves CO₂ loading. However, data in Table 7 indicate that higher airflow rates can lead to increased bed air velocity, which may reduce CO₂ capture efficiency. An optimal airflow rate of 0.298 kmol/s was selected to maintain high capture efficiency. Figure 34. Breakthrough curve modelling results at different adsorption air flowrates for 100 kg sorbent bed. The data in Table 7 also indicate that increased airflow rates result in significantly higher pressure drops, which could raise the operational cost due to the increased power requirements for adsorption blowers. To address this, two additional parameters were studied to reduce the pressure drop within the bed. Table 8 presents the variation in sorbent loading, capture efficiency, and pressure drop as a function of external voidage. As observed, increasing the void space within the bed—by reducing the backing density of the sorbent—significantly lowers the pressure drop. Importantly, the CO₂ loading capacity and capture efficiency remain nearly unchanged, since the adsorption airflow rate is maintained. Table 7.
